comparison: Perfect agreement on behavioral findings (C24-C40). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers found the statistical evidence for cue validity effects on RT and accuracy to be convincing and well-supported. No concerns were raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on SSVEP validity (C43-C47, C73-C74). Both evaluations accepted that SSVEP tracks contrast and predicts behavior, with peer reviewers praising the experimental design that allows clean separation of EEG signals.

Perfect agreement on post-response analyses (C62-C66). Both evaluations accepted the null findings regarding post-decisional confirmation bias. OpenEval noted appropriate use of both frequentist and Bayesian analyses; peer reviewers did not challenge these findings.

Agreement on motor preparation findings (C4, C55-C57). Both evaluations found the motor beta lateralization results well-supported. OpenEval emphasized the lack of task exposure effects; peer reviewers uniformly accepted that motor preparation was affected by expectations without critique.

Agreement on absence of anticipatory sensory effects (C48). Both evaluations accepted this null finding. OpenEval noted it was appropriately reported; peer reviewers implicitly accepted it without challenge.

Agreement on alpha oscillation findings (C67-C70, C87-C90). Both evaluations found evidence for differential engagement across cue conditions convincing. Peer reviewers positively received the finding and noted consistency with attention deployment when expectations are unavailable.

Agreement on task difficulty manipulation (C41-C42). Both evaluations accepted the findings about contrast reduction and performance stability. OpenEval noted relevance for interpreting sensory modulation emergence; peer reviewers did not challenge the underlying data.

Disagreement on mechanistic interpretations (C5, C8, C76, C96-C98). OpenEval rated these claims as UNCERTAIN, noting they are speculative and go beyond what data demonstrate. Peer reviewers also rated UNCERTAIN but were more critical, specifically noting lack of formal drift diffusion modeling and questioning the drift rate interpretation based on response quantile plots.

Significant disagreement on SSVEP temporal dynamics during evidence presentation (C7, C58-C61, C94). OpenEval found the evidence SUPPORTED with robust statistical models showing cue×task exposure interaction. Peer reviewers rated UNCERTAIN, raising substantial concerns about timing of SSVEP measurement relative to responses and questioning whether measured signals actually indexed evidence used for decisions.

Disagreement on interpretation of cue effects on SSVEP (C53-C54). OpenEval found the pattern of invalid cue suppression well-documented and SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers rated UNCERTAIN, specifically noting inability to determine whether effects arose from target enhancement, non-target suppression, or combinations thereof.

Partial overlap on sensory modulation claims (C49-C52, C75). OpenEval found clear evidence SUPPORTED that cues modulate sensory encoding during evidence presentation. Peer reviewers rated overlapping claims (including these) as UNCERTAIN due to concerns about SSVEP measurement timing and interpretation of what signals represent.

Agreement on methodological limitations (C99-C102). OpenEval rated the literature review and contextualization as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers explicitly endorsed the authors' acknowledgment of confounding between stimulus expectations and response expectations, viewing this transparency positively.

OpenEval evaluated sample characteristics and frequency bias issues (C108-C111, C116-C120) as SUPPORTED, commending transparency while noting small sample size limits generalizability. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these methodological details.
